meta.title: Who really said "Faith is taking the first step even when you don't see the whole staircase"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Popularly pinned on MLK, but this exact sentence appears in none of his speeches or writings. The metaphor traces to Marian Wright Edelman's 1986 recollections.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Faith is taking the first step even when you don't see the whole staircase'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to MLK, but the exact wording is in none of his documented works. It's a later paraphrase of a metaphor recalled by Marian Wright Edelman.

answer.label: Not a documented King quote — a later paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The idea may genuinely be King’s: Marian Wright Edelman, who knew him, recalled him using a partial-staircase metaphor about faith. But this exact polished sentence appears in none of his documented speeches or writings — per Quote Investigator ↗, it is a later paraphrase whose earliest trace is Edelman’s 1986 recollection, not King’s own words.

source.excerpt: “He introduced me to the idea of taking one step, even if you can’t see the whole stairway when you start.”
trail: The definitive investigation is Quote Investigator ↗, which found the line in none of King’s writings or speeches and traced it to Marian Wright Edelman.
Edelman, founder of the Children’s Defense Fund, recalled the metaphor in the 1986 Cleveland Plain Dealer interview ↗ — as a paraphrase of King’s idea, not a verbatim quote.
Popular quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ circulate the polished sentence under King’s name with no primary source attached.
source.excerptNote: Marian Wright Edelman’s 1986 recollection — the earliest published trace — is a paraphrase of King’s idea, not a direct quotation. The tidy “Faith is taking the first step…” sentence hardened later.

source.rightsNote: This exact sentence cannot be tied to any dated, published work by King — its earliest trace is a 1986 secondhand paraphrase, and the polished wording appears to be anonymous and later. With no identifiable source work or first-publication date, no copyright status can honestly be asserted; the underlying idea is credited to King (d. 1968) but the wording’s origin is unknown.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was the foremost leader of the American civil-rights movement and a Baptist minister whose sermons and speeches — from the 1963 “I Have a Dream” address to the 1968 “Mountaintop” speech — are among the most quoted in modern history. That fame makes him a magnet for feel-good lines he never actually spoke. The staircase-of-faith metaphor is credibly linked to him through a colleague’s memory, but the exact sentence circulated online is not found in his own recorded words.

misattribution.heading: How the attribution really works
misattribution.intro: The line is universally captioned “— Martin Luther King Jr.” on posters and social media, but the situation is more subtle than a clean quote or a clean fabrication.

items.why: The sentence “Faith is taking the first step even when you don’t see the whole staircase” has not been found in any of King’s speeches, sermons, or writings, per Quote Investigator ↗. It is a later, smoothed-out paraphrase.

items.who: Plausibly King, via Marian Wright Edelman
items.why: Edelman, who knew King, recalled him using a partial-staircase metaphor about faith — first in print in a 1986 interview ↗. That gives the idea real credibility, but as a memory, not a transcript.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the metaphor may well be King’s, but this polished sentence is not his documented words — the earliest evidence is Marian Wright Edelman’s 1986 recollection, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to King
lead: A concise, uplifting sentence about faith and courage is exactly the kind of line the internet gravitates toward — and Martin Luther King Jr. is one of its most reliable magnets for such lines. The staircase image is genuinely evocative and genuinely King-adjacent, which is why it spread so effectively without anyone checking a transcript.

What makes this case unusual is that the attribution isn’t baseless: a credible witness who knew King recalled him using the metaphor. The failure is one of precision — a remembered idea got quoted as if it were a verbatim line King wrote down.
context.pull: The metaphor may be King’s; the sentence is not his documented words.
